meta.title: Who really said "Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket fired signifies, in the final sense, a theft from those who hunger and are not fed, those who are cold and are not clothed"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Eisenhower really said it — in "The Chance for Peace," his 16 April 1953 address to newspaper editors, not the 1961 military-industrial complex farewell.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket fired signifies, in the final sense, a theft from those who hunger and are not fed, those who are cold and are not clothed'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Eisenhower's "Cross of Iron" speech, 16 April 1953 — not his 1961 farewell. Full passage, primary transcripts, and the common mix-ups.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1890–1969 · 34th U.S. President · Supreme Allied Commander, Europe
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed word-for-word in the transcript of “The Chance for Peace,” the address Eisenhower delivered to the American Society of Newspaper Editors in Washington, D.C., on 16 April 1953 — the speech better known as “Cross of Iron.” It is not from his 1961 farewell address, which is the speech that contains “military-industrial complex.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 16 April 1953 — American Society of Newspaper Editors, broadcast from the Statler Hotel, Washington, D.C.
The “Cross of Iron” speech, after its closing image, which echoed William Jennings Bryan’s “Cross of Gold”
Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: Dwight D. Eisenhower, 1953

source.excerpt: Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket fired signifies, in the final sense, a theft from those who hunger and are not fed, those who are cold and are not clothed. This world in arms is not spending money alone. It is spending the sweat of its laborers, the genius of its scientists, the hopes of its children. The cost of one modern heavy bomber is this: a modern brick school in more than 30 cities. It is two electric power plants, each serving a town of 60,000 population. It is two fine, fully equipped hospitals. It is some 50 miles of concrete highway. We pay for a single fighter plane with a half million bushels of wheat. We pay for a single destroyer with new homes that could have housed more than 8,000 people. This, I repeat, is the best way of life to be found on the road the world has been taking. This is not a way of life at all, in any true sense. Under the cloud of threatening war, it is humanity hanging from a cross of iron.
trail: The sentence appears verbatim in the American Presidency Project’s transcript of the 16 April 1953 address ↗ to the American Society of Newspaper Editors in Washington, D.C.
Wikisource’s full text ↗ and the Miller Center’s transcript ↗ carry the identical wording and continue the passage to “humanity hanging from a cross of iron.”
Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ cites it to “The Chance for Peace,” speech to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, 16 April 1953 — the same speech and date.

Specialist quote investigator Professor Buzzkill returned a genuine-quote verdict ↗ for this line, matching the same source and date and naming Emmet Hughes as Eisenhower’s speechwriter for the occasion.
source.excerptNote: Eisenhower underlined the word theft in his speaking copy, according to Professor Buzzkill’s account of the speech ↗.

author.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
author.heading: Who was Eisenhower?
author.metaLine: 1890–1969 · Five-star general · 34th President of the United States
author.bio: Dwight David Eisenhower was born in Denison, Texas, in 1890 and rose to Supreme Commander of the Allied Expeditionary Force, the post he held from December 1943 through the Normandy landings to July 1945. He then served as Army Chief of Staff, president of Columbia University, and the first Supreme Allied Commander of NATO before winning the presidency, which he held from January 1953 to January 1961. That résumé is exactly what gives this line its force: the arithmetic of guns-versus-schoolhouses is being done by the man who had run the largest military operation in history.

misattribution.heading: Right man, wrong speech
misattribution.intro: The attribution itself is solid — Eisenhower said this, on the record, in front of the country’s newspaper editors. What goes wrong is almost always the where and when, and the amount of speech that gets left behind.

items.why: The line is routinely filed under the “military-industrial complex” farewell — a mix-up Professor Buzzkill flags directly ↗. That farewell was delivered on 17 January 1961 ↗ and is where the phrase “military-industrial complex” appears; the “every gun” passage belongs to the 1953 address, eight years earlier.

Reposts of the full text circulate under a 1956 date — one widely copied version headlines it ‘Cross of Iron’ Speech 1956 ↗ while reproducing the genuine 1953 text. The nickname is real; the year is not.

Quoted alone, it reads as a blanket pacifist statement. Professor Buzzkill calculates ↗ that the peace-themed section is about 9% of the roughly 3,000-word substantive speech — the rest is a hard-edged Cold War argument aimed at the new Soviet leadership.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording is authentic and the speaker is right: it is Eisenhower, from “The Chance for Peace,” 16 April 1953 ↗ — cite that address, not the farewell, and not 1956.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Eisenhower gave this speech weeks after Joseph Stalin’s death, at a moment when the new Soviet leadership seemed briefly negotiable and the Korean War was still running. The pitch was disarmament, and the rhetorical move that made it stick was accounting: he did not argue that weapons were immoral, he priced them. One heavy bomber, he told the editors, equals “a modern brick school in more than 30 cities”; a single destroyer equals homes for more than 8,000 people.

The closing image borrowed from William Jennings Bryan’s “Cross of Gold” — “humanity hanging from a cross of iron” — which is why the address is remembered under the nickname “Cross of Iron.” Coming from a five-star general in his first months as president, the passage has been quoted by peace movements and defence hawks alike ever since, usually without the Cold War framing that surrounded it.
context.detailsSummary: How the passage came to be written
detailsBody: Eisenhower’s principal speechwriter for the address was Emmet Hughes, assisted by Robert Kieve, according to Professor Buzzkill’s investigation of the quote ↗, which traces the speech’s central guns-versus-butter theme to an Oval Office moment when Eisenhower watched an F-86 Sabre and began reckoning its cost against what the money could otherwise buy.
The same investigation notes that Eisenhower underlined the word theft in his speaking copy — the accusation was deliberate, not a slip of oratory.
